The invitation extended to me by the Editors to contribute to this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry, centered on embodiment, made me realize that I had never explicitly addressed the subject. And so in this essay, without contextualizing my thoughts about embodiment in the large, existing literature on the topic, I begin to think through the relation of embodiment to the phenomena I have described over the course of the last forty years or so: unformulated experience, dissociation, enactment, and the interpersonal field. I also take up the relation of the verbal and the nonverbal, arguing that to grant a fundamental role to the body in psychoanalysis does not imply that language is secondary. I go on to present a schematic understanding of the role of embodied processes in the formulation of experience, and I end with an illustration of somatic life in clinical process.

In recent years the noun “other” has worked its way through the culture and emerged as the verb “to other” – meaning to reduce someone to a mere external representation, lacking depth and interiority, and thus easing the way for us to discount or destroy that person. The phenomenon of othering goes so against the ethos of our psychoanalytic tribe (which claims to self the other, as opposed to other the self) and yet has become such a prominent experience in our world that many of us have put the problem of the other on a par with that of the self, a problem that lights up core values in our field and core vulnerabilities in the individual. The writers in this issue have confronted the problem from two positions, one positive, one negative. We can describe the two positions by the questions they bring up. On the positive side, what does it mean to try to know or love an other as one would know or love oneself? What does that do for the other? What does that do for the self? On the negative side, what does it mean to other a person or a group? What does that do to the other? What does that do to the self?

John Riker opens the issue with a bird’s eye view of the self/other problem from the perspective of Hegel, who sees the human animal as split between being a subject and an object. As subjects, we are “sheer openness” and feel ourselves to be infinite. As objects, we are finite mortals, formed by social and physical forces, not so much free as defined, prejudiced, limited in vision. For Hegel, the self-consciousness necessary for a human being to become a subject depends on recognition by others, leading to a futile life and death struggle through history in which one will emerge as a “master” and another as a “slave,” but in which neither is free, as neither can be fully recognized by the other. Hegel’s answer: the management of desire by a rational mind devoted to a universal ideal of mutual recognition. In an important critique, Riker argues that Hegel (and Freud for that matter) failed to take into account a tendency for the master/slave dynamic to split around core differences – of skin tone, of religion, etc. Our aggression is not random but toward “the other.” Riker finds a partial answer in Kohut’s concept of the twinship transference, which describes our fundamental human need to be in companionship with people we perceive as just like us; therein lies our tendency to experience otherness as a narcissistic blow. He begins the task of finding ways to bridge the gap – felt often as a wound – opened up by otherness.

This article is about the adaptive function of dreams. It applies Hartmann’s descriptions of autonomous ego functions, especially the synthetic function of the ego, to the dream’s use of reality and to the use of dreams for adaptation; to reality and to neurotic conflict. Humans are fundamentally embodied! Analysts, starting with Freud, have implicitly endorsed this statement. Yet, it is only within the last two decades that conjectures about the ways in which embodiment affects psychoanalytic theory and practice have appeared in our literature. In this issue we have gathered articles by some of the leading proponents of what we see as a widespread movement toward an embodied perspective in psychoanalysis.

The variety of the authors’ takes on embodiment reflect how difficult it is to pin down exactly what makes the concept so important for our thinking and our work. It may well be that all the approaches are needed.

It seems fitting to begin this issue with an introduction by Melvin Bornstein to a brief commentary and two clinical “stories” that Joseph Lichtenberg sent to us only months before he died. His inspiring commitment to embodiment is exemplified in these unfinished pieces.

Donnel Stern has advanced some of the most widely used concepts in contemporary psychoanalysis including “unformulated experience,” “dissociative enactment” and “the interpersonal field.” It is the relation of these phenomena to embodiment that Stern explores for the first time in his article. He persuasively argues that positing the fundamental role played by the nonverbal does not detract from the importance of the verbal. His clinical example illustrates the role of embodied processes in the formulation of experience.

Siri Gullestad sees the new emphasis on embodiment as stemming from cognitive science research. However, she traces its deep roots in psychoanalysis back to the Norwegian character analytic tradition that emphasizes nonverbal behavior and “body language.” Through her clinical example, she explores how a patient’s embodied, structuralized bearing and bodily appearance reveal relational messages. She introduces her concept of “relational scenario” as a helpful way to observe transference-countertransference dynamics.

Using two clinical vignettes as illustration, William Cornell demonstrates how somatic receptivity and interventions can prove healing for patients who experience severe levels of disembodiment. He contrasts what he refers to as splits in mind-body with interpersonal/transference interpretations. Cornell draws on the work of Lombardi, Alvarez, and Bucci in support of his emphasis on the therapist’s need to pay primary attention to mind-body splits.

This article explores various dimensions of the case presentation, especially connections with Searles’ extensive interviews with Robert Langs, which provide much relevant personal and professional background for his work with Joan Douglas. Since Searles told me in 2000 that he believed some of his previous patients actually had multiple personality, I explore what Searles once called multiple identity functioning in Joan. I also respond to selected topics presented in the other commentary articles in this issue. Estelle Shane is a distinguished psychoanalyst, who has honored, served, and contributed to the profession. During my training and early years as an analyst, she was my teacher and mentor, and over time she has become my close colleague and friend. I admire and love her balanced temperament, her ever growing mind and heart, her genuine kindness and unique shine, but I’m also occasionally exasperated - as friends are - at some of her patterned foibles. Despite a long and rich life, Estelle still wants so much; she’s greedy for more - more work, writing, ideas, articles, books, movies, theater, and interesting and challenging patients, colleagues and friends. She wants more intense intellectual and emotional experience, more intellectual and emotional understanding - More Life and More Time. And she tries to schedule it all in. Even during Covid sequestration, Estelle is at war with time. Therapy sessions, tea parties and coffee klatches, consultations, private conversations, editor meetings, writing lessons - all these continue online in her familiar pace and race, and Estelle logs in more ZOOM and FACETIME miles than anybody I know. In her pursuit of life and her battle with time, she overcommits herself, is often overwhelmed by her own chosen obligations, and frequently must extricate herself from too many overlapping dates. How many times has Estelle canceled an appointment because she has inadvertently scheduled two other people in my time slot? Exasperating, but by now also inspiring; that is, even though I have to share her, I love how large and curious and hungry for life she is. So now she and I are going to have a conversation about minds: what they are in all their eccentric patterns and shifts, how we understand our own and the other’s, how we use them, and how they function in analytic work. Estelle’s theories are well documented in her writings, and so I want to go beyond her theories to talk about what she actually does with her patients and how she has come to think about analytic practice.

Misogyny, feminine body, female sexuality, phallic monism, repudiation of femininity, phallic mother, faecal defenses

Misogyny as evoked in the mother-daughter relationship is presented here in the repudiation and debasement of the feminine sexual body. It is explored as it relates to phallic monism via the clinical case of Iphigeneia and the mythical Greek female character of the same name in Euripides’ trilogy. The unconscious loyalty and submission to the pregenital phallic mother (Sphinx) is suggested to constitute one reason for phallic monism. Women’s misogyny towards their own sexual bodies due to their unconscious loyalty and submission to the Sphinx is explored. This representation of the Sphinx (borrowed by Schaeffer, 2011) is evoked to stand for the harsh/primitive phallic maternal imago who does not allow her daughter’s independence and passing into the world of adulthood and genital sexuality.

We came to examining the spiritual dimension of psychoanalysis from two directions. Since the reader is likely to locate themself somewhere in-between the two of us, we thought including our two separate accounts might provide an orienting map for the issue.

Daniel Goldin

I grew up culturally Jewish in an atheist household. I remember reading a children’s version of the Bible for its stories alongside Grimm’s Fairy Tales. I knew even then that institutional religion was for non-enlightened people willing to believe these childish stories into adulthood. And yet I remained drawn to those men and women who fought lions and saw burning bushes and wrestled with angels. The feelings were real, even if the incidents were not. I remember checking out a temple with my first wife after the birth of our first child, both of us longing at that moment for some contact with our ancestors. We pushed through the heavy doors, listened to the Hebrew prayers, watched the people davening - and then rushed back out into the anonymous street-life. The temple would always be taboo for me. I think I came to psychoanalysis as a kind of compromise. Here was a secular project that gave pride of place to the invisible. What my patients and I come up with together has no existence in the brain nor in the world, but comes into being only between minds. Whether we think of this “something” as a narrative or as an emergent property of an intersubjective exchange, one thing we can be certain of is that it is immaterial. It may not be spiritual, but it is spiritual-adjacent.

Steven Barrie-Anthony

I grew up in a household steeped in eastern mysticism. My parents were seekers who believed that God is what’s deepest within us. Versions of this intimate nondual divine populate mysticisms throughout the world’s religious traditions, and I grew up feeling connected to a mystical core that I saw as cutting across divisions. Although my spirituality bent inward and resisted capture in terms of doctrines and institutions, it didn’t feel, as William James saw it, solitary. In fact, while I often rejected merging my spirituality with labels and social commitments, the spiritual to me felt innately connective and relational. Not just words on the page but relationships with the poets; intimate contact between friends and family that dipped us for a moment into divinity, and then something of that contact kept on resounding within. I was a scholar of religion before becoming a psychoanalyst. When, in my Ph.D. dissertation, I wrote about “inner connections,” my sociologist adviser asked quizzically whether that’s a contradiction - don’t inner spiritual experiences, and sociological connections, move on different planes? Paradox and possible at once, I think. I came to psychoanalysis in part because it’s a space where these different planes can at times join up.

In this paper I propose that reaching the limits of our ordinary ways of knowing as psychoanalysts can offer thresholds into new and vast experiences of transformation. I explore how emotional experiences of not knowing have their own authority in creating intimacy in the analytic dyad and an experience of transcendence. I use three clinical examples including my own experience as a patient to illustrate this.

Ethics, ethical values, transcendence, love of unique being, Levinas, Chetrit-Vatine, Dante

Freud’s understanding of science allowed no origin for commitment to ethical values except via the superego. Recently, some psychoanalysts have found a more persuasive source in the thought of Emmanuel Levinas. In this paper, using in particular Viviane Chetrit-Vatine’s notion of “matricial space,” I attempt to look further at the implications of Levinas’s idea of “transcendence,” not as something special but as the ordinary horizon of seriously-held ethical values. To work as such, it must involve an affective dimension. Referencing Derrida’s Adieu for Levinas, I discuss this in terms of different meanings of the word “love,” in particular a certain sort of love for the unique “being” of the other, rather than for his or her “doing.”

Reparation, surrender, mourning, truth, transformation, co-suffering

This essay explores the psychological and spiritual process of our ability to surrender, accept that which we cannot change or repair, and to mourn. This process stands in tension within us between the unconscious pull to relive things that went wrong, to relive them and attempt to do them right this time, and to heal ourselves through reparation. A contemporary perspective tries to break those binary models of mind and acknowledges that we live in constant tension between the wish to avoid and the capacity to bear the pain and losses that life brings. In this essay I explore the latter. When we surrender, when we accept that which cannot be changed or fixed, we touch an emotional truth that allows us to start mourning. That permission to grieve for our losses and faults connects us with life and welcomes the birth of new possibilities.

“In conformity with its peculiar nature, psycho-analysis does not try to describe what a woman is - that would be a task it could scarcely perform - but sets about enquiring how she comes into being.”

~ Freud, Lecture 33: Femininity

“One is not born a woman, but becomes one.”

~ De Beauvoir, Second Sex

“Get thee to a nunnery, go. Farewell. Or, if thou wilt needs marry, marry a fool; wise men know well enough what monsters you make of them. To a nunnery, go, and quickly too. Farewell. … I have heard of your paintings too, well enough; God has given you one face, and you make yourselves another. You jig, you amble, and you lisp, you nick-name God’s creatures, and make your wantonness your ignorance. Go to, I’ll no more on it; it hath made me mad.”

~ Shakespeare: Hamlet to Ophelia

In the current moment - amid the long-deferred, now crucial and painful reckoning with our collective and individual racism, amid our nuanced, shifting recognition of the complexity within gender identity and sexuality - the persistent and insidious nature of misogyny appears to take a back seat. Misogyny, both the experience and the impact, can easily get lost; after all, women, especially heterosexual, white women, seem to enjoy ostensible and broad privileges and protections. As such, the consequences of misogyny and the resultant suffering might appear, well, inconsequential. Playing out in ordinary ways in everyday life, misogyny is often viewed and treated as if it were a less egregious, significant and harmful form of discrimination and hatred - an insult, perhaps, rather than an injury, an appreciative pat on the backside, not an annihilating assault. Yet, as most dramatically and immediately exemplified by the on-going abortion rights debate, a woman’s life and choices concerning the quality of her life, her body and her opportunities are frequently perceived as less important - a secondary consideration, if considered at all.1

Surely, there are numerous, multidimensional, and interlacing explanations and theories about what holds this tenacious form of hatred and discrimination in place, despite one feminist wave after another. We could speculate, for example, that misogyny arises as a natural but pernicious byproduct of, or response to, the fundamental anthropological situation: the powerful mother (so it seems to the powerless infant) holds the key to life. She has the ability and the desire to beckon the child into life.2 That the maternal, as represented by the female of the species, also represents a puissant presence may account for the indifference with which misogyny is perceived: a woman’s power, authority and agency are taken as a given, taken for granted - and, thus, threats to that power are devalued just as a woman’s prima facie power is overvalued.
